read.sections.0.heading.source: Everyday work can become a major subject
read.sections.0.heading.back: Everyday work can become the main subject

read.sections.0.text.source:
Art does not show only rulers, famous events or extraordinary people. Artists have also pictured farming, preparing food, caring for others, travel and rest. These subjects make ordinary labour, or work done by people, visible. The ways that artworks were commissioned, sold and displayed also connect their subjects with the people who could afford to own them.

You saw The Harvesters in Lesson 1. Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it in 1565, and he arranged workers across a landscape. Some gather grain; others eat or rest under a tree. The Met's family guide connects the picture with the traditional theme of work through the seasons. Distant houses, a church and boats place the harvest within a larger world where people live. The labour of producing food and everyday life share the same scene.
read.sections.0.text.note: glossary "labour" = แรงงาน (not in KEY_TERMS). It also means "workers/workforce" in Thai; check it reads as work done by people.
read.sections.0.text.back:
Art does not only show rulers, famous events or extraordinary people. Artists also painted farming, preparing food, caring for others, travelling and resting. These subjects make ordinary labour, or the work people do, something visible. The way works were commissioned, sold and displayed also connects the subject of the picture with the people who had enough money to own the work.

You saw The Harvesters in Lesson 1. Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it in 1565, placing workers all over the landscape. Some are gathering the grain, some are eating or resting under a tree. The Metropolitan Museum of Art's family guide connects this picture with the traditional subject of the work of each season. The houses, church and boats in the distance place the harvest in a wider world where people live. The labour of producing food and daily life are in the same scene.

read.sections.1.heading.source: A merchant's picture of farm work
read.sections.1.heading.back: A merchant's picture of farm work

read.sections.1.text.source:
The Met's collection record says that an Antwerp merchant commissioned the painting for his country house. He was its patron, the person who paid for it. The museum describes the workers as shown with sympathy, but idealised: presented as more orderly and perfect than real life. The painting's first owner and the farm workers in it had very different places in society. Its ordered plenty is one way of presenting rural life, not a complete record of it.

Bruegel's setting belongs to the southern Low Countries, including land that is now in Belgium. Antwerp was a major port and art market. The Met describes how trade and cultural contacts attracted artists and supported workshops. They also encouraged artists to make works for buyers beyond one town. A picture of the countryside could therefore belong to a business world in the city. This is context for the commission. It does not mean that every farmer shared the merchant's wealth, or that one painting represents all European life.
read.sections.1.text.note: glossary "idealisation" = แบบอุดมคติ (as in ศิลปะแบบอุดมคติ), used as "เป็นแบบอุดมคติ" / "วาดแบบอุดมคติ". Not in KEY_TERMS; a child may not know อุดมคติ, so the text explains it each time. Check.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art's record says a merchant in Antwerp commissioned this picture for his country house. He was the picture's patron, the person who paid for it to be made. The museum explains that the workers in the picture are painted with sympathy but idealised, that is, they look more orderly and perfect than real life. The first owner of the picture and the field workers in the picture had very different places in society. The orderly abundance in the picture is one way of presenting country life, not a complete record of that life.

The scene of Bruegel's picture is in the southern Low Countries, which include the land that is now Belgium. Antwerp was an important port city and art market. The Metropolitan Museum of Art explains that trade and cultural contact attracted artists and helped support workshops. These things also encouraged artists to make works for buyers outside their own city. So a country picture could be part of a city business world. This is the context of the commission; it does not mean every peasant was as rich as the merchant, or that a single painting represents all of life in Europe.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
The museum says a trader in Antwerp paid for the painting. He was its patron. A patron pays for a work. It hung in his country house. The museum says the workers are shown kindly. But they are idealised. That means they look neater and better than in real life. The rich owner and the farm workers had very different lives. So the painting shows one view of farm life, not all of it.

Antwerp was in the southern Low Countries. Today that land is in Belgium. Antwerp was a busy port. Art was bought and sold there. Artists came for work. They made art for buyers in many towns. So a picture of farm work could belong to a rich city world. This does not mean every farmer was rich. And one painting does not show all of Europe.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
The museum says a merchant in Antwerp paid for this picture to be painted. He was the picture's patron. A patron is the person who pays for a work to be made. The picture hung in his country house. The museum says the picture shows the workers kindly, but the workers are idealised, that is, they look neater and better than real life. The rich owner and the field workers had very different lives. So this picture shows one kind of farm life, not all of it.

Antwerp was in the southern Low Countries. Today that land is in Belgium. Antwerp was a busy port city. Art was bought and sold there. Artists came to look for work here. They made works for buyers in many cities. So a picture of farm work could be part of a rich city world. But this does not mean every peasant was rich, and one picture does not show all of Europe.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Prints for a new group of buyers

read.sections.2.text.source:
Almost three centuries later, Jean-François Millet made an etching called The Gleaners. An etching is a print made from a prepared metal plate. The National Gallery of Art's example dates to 1855. Three figures bend to gather crops left over after the harvest. This lesson uses the print, not Millet's better-known oil painting of a related subject from 1857. Fine lines, repeated poses and the way the figures sit in the field organise the viewer's attention.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum holds another example of the etching and explains its market. Millet began making prints in the mid-1850s, partly to earn money and to reach possible buyers. Pictures of the countryside appealed to middle-class ideas about the dignity of work. Such calm, reassuring pictures could exist alongside fears of social conflict after the upheavals of 1848. What an artwork shows and why its audience valued it are not always the same.

These examples connect art with food, labour, class and the market for pictures. A wealthy buyer could admire a picture of work without sharing the worker's life. An artist could make workers important while also needing buyers. Neither relationship automatically makes the art dishonest. It makes production and ownership part of its history. Dates, materials, patrons and markets help explain why pictures of ordinary labour belonged in collections as well as in the fields they showed.
read.sections.2.text.note: etching = ภาพพิมพ์กัดกรด (the Thai art-class term). middle-class = ชนชั้นกลาง; dignity of work = งานเป็นสิ่งที่มีศักดิ์ศรี. Sentence ends on a year moved or padded (ที่ผ่านมา) because the checker cannot split a sentence after a number.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Almost three centuries later, Jean-François Millet made an etching called The Gleaners. An etching is a print made from a prepared metal plate. The National Gallery of Art, Washington's print is from 1855. In the picture, three people bend down to gather crops left over after the harvest. This lesson uses the print, not Millet's more famous oil painting of a similar subject from 1857. Fine lines, repeated poses and the positions of the people in the field help arrange the viewer's eye.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art has another impression of this etching and explains the market for the picture. Millet began making prints in the mid-1850s, partly to earn money and to reach people who might buy pictures. Country pictures appealed to middle-class people who thought work was something dignified. Calm, comforting pictures like this existed alongside fear of social conflict after the unrest of 1848. What a work shows and why viewers value it are not always the same.

These examples connect art with food, labour, class and the market for pictures. Rich buyers could admire pictures of work without living like workers. An artist could make workers look important and at the same time need buyers. Neither relationship automatically makes the art insincere, but it makes production and ownership part of the work's history. The date, material, patron and market help explain why pictures of ordinary labour ended up in collections, besides in the fields the pictures show.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Almost 300 years later, Millet made The Gleaners. It is an etching. An etching is a print made from a metal plate. This one is from 1855. Three people bend down. They pick up crops left after the harvest. This is the print, not his famous painting from 1857. Thin lines and the same bent shapes guide our eyes.

Another museum has a copy of this etching. It says Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints helped him find buyers. Many buyers were middle class. They liked the idea that farm work was good and honest. These calm pictures sold at a time of fear. People worried about conflict after the troubles of 1848. So why people liked a picture can differ from what it shows.

A rich buyer could like a picture of work without doing that work. An artist could show workers with respect and still need buyers. That does not make the art false. It means making and owning art are part of its story. Dates, materials, patrons and buyers all help explain these pictures of labour.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Almost 300 years later, Millet made The Gleaners. This picture is an etching. An etching is a print made from a metal plate. This picture is from 1855. In the picture three people bend down. They gather the crops left after the harvest. This is the print, not the famous painting from 1857. Thin lines and the same bending pose help guide our eye.

Another museum has another impression of this print. The museum says Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints helped him find buyers. Many buyers were middle-class people. They liked the idea that farm work was good and honest work. These calm pictures sold at a time when people were afraid. In 1848 there was unrest. After that people worried about conflict. So the reason people like a picture can be different from what the picture shows.

Rich buyers could like pictures of work without doing that work themselves. An artist could show workers with respect and still need buyers. This does not make the art fake, but it means making and owning are part of the work's story. The date, the material, the patron and the buyers help explain these pictures of labour.

write.example.source: Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints also helped him reach new buyers. Many of his buyers were middle-class people, not farm workers. They liked pictures of the countryside because of their own ideas about the dignity of work. So The Gleaners shows three people bending in a field. But it was made to be sold to people whose lives were very different from theirs.
write.example.back: Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints also helped him reach new groups of buyers. Many of his buyers were middle-class people, not field workers. They liked country pictures because of their own idea that work is dignified. So The Gleaners shows three people bending in a field, but it was made to sell to people whose lives were very different from the people in the picture.
